iLQR and Differential Dynamic Programming

A boat approaching a quay must arrive in the right place, face along the berth, and lose its remaining momentum. A sequence of thrust commands determines all three outcomes. The shooting formulation turns this task into an optimization over those commands: simulate a candidate sequence, measure its cost, and improve it. How can an optimizer use the time structure of the simulation when computing that improvement?

Linearizing the dynamics along the current trajectory and quadratically approximating its costs gives a problem whose controls can be eliminated backward, one time step at a time. The resulting correction is then tested through the nonlinear simulator. Repeating these operations gives the iterative linear-quadratic regulator, or iLQR. Keeping additional curvature from the dynamics gives differential dynamic programming, or DDP. Both methods compute corrections around the current plan. The local problem is the linear-quadratic regulator solved by dynamic programming in the previous chapter, and its backward recursion can also be read as substitution and quadratic minimization.

The chapter is a bridge between the exact dynamic programming of the previous chapter and the stochastic dynamic programming of the next. iLQR reuses the LQR backward recursion, but only locally: its quadratic models and its feedback gains describe a neighborhood of one trajectory, not the whole state space.

Learning Goals¶

After working through the derivations and examples, you should be able to:

  • Construct a local quadratic optimal-control problem around a feasible rollout.

  • Eliminate its controls backward and recover an affine correction at each step.

  • Implement nonlinear trial rollouts with line search and regularization.

  • Identify the dynamics-curvature terms that distinguish DDP from iLQR.

  • Assess a docking plan using its cost, arrival velocity, and hull clearance.

  • Explain how thermal load and nonlinear power loss shape a bounded cooling schedule.

Prerequisites¶

The chapter uses the finite-horizon optimal-control formulation, single shooting, the linear-quadratic regulator from finite-horizon dynamic programming, and first and second derivatives. The SQP section of the nonlinear-programming appendix introduces general SQP subproblems, and the initial-value-problem appendix reviews numerical integration.

A Docking Problem¶

Docking requires the boat to reach the berth, align with the quay, and shed its momentum. If the boat reaches the right position with appreciable translational or angular velocity, its momentum will carry it away again.

Consider a two-metre boat moving in the horizontal plane. Its state and control are

x=(px,py,ψ,vx,vy,ω),u=(uL,uR)∈[−1,1]2.\mathbf x=(p_x,p_y,\psi,v_x,v_y,\omega),\qquad \mathbf u=(u_L,u_R)\in[-1,1]^2.x=(px​,py​,ψ,vx​,vy​,ω),u=(uL​,uR​)∈[−1,1]2.
(1)

The position and velocity are measured in fixed world coordinates, ψ\psiψ is the heading, and ω\omegaω is the angular velocity. Each control is a fraction of maximum thrust. Positive commands push forward and negative commands push backward. Unequal thrusts turn the boat. There is no directly commanded sideways force, so an approach with sideways momentum requires a maneuver.

Let e(ψ)=(cos⁡ψ,sin⁡ψ)⊤\mathbf e(\psi)=(\cos\psi,\sin\psi)^\tope(ψ)=(cosψ,sinψ)⊤ point along the boat and n(ψ)=(−sin⁡ψ,cos⁡ψ)⊤\mathbf n(\psi)=(-\sin\psi,\cos\psi)^\topn(ψ)=(−sinψ,cosψ)⊤ point across it. The simplified inertial model is

p˙=v,ψ˙=ω,mv˙=Fmax⁡(uL+uR)e−d∥(e⊤v)e−d⊥(n⊤v)n,Iω˙=bFmax⁡(uR−uL)−dωω.\begin{aligned} \dot{\mathbf p}&=\mathbf v,&\qquad \dot\psi&=\omega,\\ m\dot{\mathbf v} &=F_{\max}(u_L+u_R)\mathbf e -d_\parallel(\mathbf e^\top\mathbf v)\mathbf e -d_\perp(\mathbf n^\top\mathbf v)\mathbf n,\\ I\dot\omega&=bF_{\max}(u_R-u_L)-d_\omega\omega. \end{aligned}p˙​mv˙Iω˙​=v,=Fmax​(uL​+uR​)e−d∥​(e⊤v)e−d⊥​(n⊤v)n,=bFmax​(uR​−uL​)−dω​ω.​ψ˙​=ω,

This is a smooth penalty for violating the buffer. Its finite weight permits violations, so the final trajectories will also undergo a separate geometric clearance check. The full rectangle is used for that check, including the area outside the pointed boat icon in the figures.

(4)

These numerical weights apply to the stated SI coordinates and dimensionless thrust commands. The periodic heading penalty assigns the same cost to angles that differ by a full turn. The simulator retains an unwrapped angle; it does not insert a discontinuity at ±π\pm\pi±π into the differentiated transition.

The initial control sequence is zero, so the boat coasts and slows under drag. It stops far from the berth. Successive control updates can first bring it closer and then adjust the arrival heading and velocity.

Taylor Models of Dynamics and Cost¶

The local model describes the change in cost caused by a small change in the thrust sequence. Start from the finite-horizon problem

min⁡UJ(U):=cT(xT)+∑t=1T−1ct(xt,ut),s.t.xt+1=ft(xt,ut),t=1,…,T−1,x1=xinit.\begin{aligned} \min_{\mathbf U}\quad &J(\mathbf U) :=c_T(\mathbf x_T)+\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}c_t(\mathbf x_t,\mathbf u_t),\\ \text{s.t.}\quad &\mathbf x_{t+1}=\mathbf f_t(\mathbf x_t,\mathbf u_t), \quad t=1,\ldots,T-1,\\ &\mathbf x_1=\mathbf x_{\mathrm{init}}. \end{aligned}Umin​s.t.​J(U):=cT​(xT​)+t=1∑T−1​ct​(xt​,ut​),xt+1​=ft​(xt​,ut​),t=1,…,T−1,x1​=xinit​.​
(5)

Here U=(u1,…,uT−1)\mathbf U=(\mathbf u_1,\ldots,\mathbf u_{T-1})U=(u1​,…,uT−1​) is the complete control sequence. Its rollout determines every later state. This is an open-loop problem: the decision variable is a sequence of commands fixed in advance, not a rule that reacts to the state. iLQR returns such a sequence. The feedback gains KtK_tKt​ that appear below are a by-product of the computation. Near the returned plan they tell how to adjust each command when the state drifts from the planned one, through u=uˉ+K(x−xˉ)\mathbf u=\bar{\mathbf u}+K(\mathbf x-\bar{\mathbf x})u=uˉ+K(x−xˉ), and they say nothing about states far from it.

Figure 2 shows what “near the plan” means. The boat follows the final docking plan and receives a small push after two seconds. Replaying the planned thrusts ignores the push. The boats drift calmly but none reaches the berth: they miss it by 0.9 m on average and by up to 2.2 m. Applying the local feedback steers all twelve pushed runs back onto the plan, and they arrive within a millimetre of it. These runs stay inside a thin tube around the planned trajectory.

The tube has a limited width. With pushes twice as large, shown in the animation below, several feedback runs leave it and two never reach the berth. Their corrections ask for more thrust than the thrusters can give, and the boat moves far enough from the plan that the linear model is no longer accurate. The gains describe a neighborhood of one trajectory, and this whole chapter works inside such neighborhoods.

We cannot solve this nonlinear problem directly. The previous chapter showed that a linear-quadratic regulator problem can be solved exactly by a backward recursion. The idea of this chapter is to build an LQR problem that resembles ours near a current plan, solve it, use its solution to improve the plan, and repeat.

Set aside the control bounds while deriving this local problem. The current plan is a control sequence Uˉ\bar{\mathbf U}Uˉ together with the states obtained by rolling it out, xˉt+1=ft(xˉt,uˉt)\bar{\mathbf x}_{t+1}=\mathbf f_t(\bar{\mathbf x}_t,\bar{\mathbf u}_t)xˉt+1​=ft​(xˉt​,uˉt​). For the boat, the first plan is the zero-thrust coast. The plan is our current guess, not a reference that the boat must track. To ask what happens if we change it, consider nudges δxt=xt−xˉt\delta\mathbf x_t=\mathbf x_t-\bar{\mathbf x}_tδxt​=xt​−xˉt​ and δut=ut−uˉt\delta\mathbf u_t=\mathbf u_t-\bar{\mathbf u}_tδut​=ut​−uˉt​, stacked as δzt=(δxt,δut)\delta\mathbf z_t=(\delta\mathbf x_t,\delta\mathbf u_t)δzt​=(δxt​,δut​). These are hypothetical changes that we are free to choose, not measured errors.

The linear model of the transition follows the usual Taylor steps. A scalar function of one variable satisfies f(a+h)≈f(a)+f′(a)hf(a+h)\approx f(a)+f'(a)hf(a+h)≈f(a)+f′(a)h. With two inputs the partial derivatives add: f(xˉ+δx,uˉ+δu)≈f(xˉ,uˉ)+∂xf δx+∂uf δuf(\bar x+\delta x,\bar u+\delta u)\approx f(\bar x,\bar u) +\partial_x f\,\delta x+\partial_u f\,\delta uf(xˉ+δx,uˉ+δu)≈f(xˉ,uˉ)+∂x​fδx+∂u​fδu. The transition ft\mathbf f_tft​ has one such expansion for each of its nxn_xnx​ components. Each component gives one row, and stacking the rows gives the Jacobian matrices AtA_tAt​ and BtB_tBt​:

ft(xˉt+δxt,uˉt+δut)=ft(xˉt,uˉt)+Atδxt+Btδut+O(∥δzt∥2),At=∂ft∂x∣(xˉt,uˉt),Bt=∂ft∂u∣(xˉt,uˉt).\begin{aligned} \mathbf f_t(\bar{\mathbf x}_t+\delta\mathbf x_t, \bar{\mathbf u}_t+\delta\mathbf u_t) &=\mathbf f_t(\bar{\mathbf x}_t,\bar{\mathbf u}_t) +A_t\delta\mathbf x_t+B_t\delta\mathbf u_t +O(\|\delta\mathbf z_t\|^2),\\ A_t&=\left.\frac{\partial\mathbf f_t}{\partial\mathbf x} \right|_{(\bar{\mathbf x}_t,\bar{\mathbf u}_t)},\\ B_t&=\left.\frac{\partial\mathbf f_t}{\partial\mathbf u} \right|_{(\bar{\mathbf x}_t,\bar{\mathbf u}_t)}. \end{aligned}ft​(xˉt​+δxt​,uˉt​+δut​)At​Bt​​=ft​(xˉt​,uˉt​)+At​δxt​+Bt​δut​+O(∥δzt​∥2),=∂x∂ft​​∣∣​(xˉt​,uˉt​)​,=∂u∂ft​​∣∣​(xˉt​,uˉt​)​.​
(6)

The left side is the transition evaluated at the nudged state and control, which is the new next state xt+1\mathbf x_{t+1}xt+1​. Because the current plan is a rollout, the first term on the right is ft(xˉt,uˉt)=xˉt+1\mathbf f_t(\bar{\mathbf x}_t,\bar{\mathbf u}_t)=\bar{\mathbf x}_{t+1}ft​(xˉt​,uˉt​)=xˉt+1​. Subtracting xˉt+1\bar{\mathbf x}_{t+1}xˉt+1​ from both sides turns the left side into δxt+1\delta\mathbf x_{t+1}δxt+1​ and cancels that term on the right. Dropping the quadratic remainder gives the linearized dynamics δxt+1=Atδxt+Btδut\delta\mathbf x_{t+1}=A_t\delta\mathbf x_t+B_t\delta\mathbf u_tδxt+1​=At​δxt​+Bt​δut​. Both rollouts start from the same state, so δx1=0\delta\mathbf x_1=\mathbf0δx1​=0. There is no constant defect because the current plan satisfies the discrete dynamics. Independently chosen state guesses would generally leave such a defect. We write Ft=[At Bt]F_t=[A_t\ B_t]Ft​=[At​ Bt​] for the combined Jacobian.

The running cost is expanded by the same steps, one order higher. In one variable, f(a+h)≈f(a)+f′(a)h+12f′′(a)h2f(a+h)\approx f(a)+f'(a)h+\tfrac12f''(a)h^2f(a+h)≈f(a)+f′(a)h+21​f′′(a)h2. The quadratic term therefore reads 12δxt⊤cxx,tδxt+δut⊤cux,tδxt+12δut⊤cuu,tδut\tfrac12\delta\mathbf x_t^\top c_{xx,t}\delta\mathbf x_t +\delta\mathbf u_t^\top c_{ux,t}\delta\mathbf x_t +\tfrac12\delta\mathbf u_t^\top c_{uu,t}\delta\mathbf u_t21​δxt⊤​cxx,t​δxt​+δut⊤​cux,t​δxt​+21​δut⊤​cuu,t​δut​, where the two mixed blocks have combined into one term. (7)

Here cˉt=ct(xˉt,uˉt)\bar c_t=c_t(\bar{\mathbf x}_t,\bar{\mathbf u}_t)cˉt​=ct​(xˉt​,uˉt​) and cx,t=∇xct(xˉt,uˉt)c_{x,t}=\nabla_{\mathbf x}c_t(\bar{\mathbf x}_t,\bar{\mathbf u}_t)cx,t​=∇x​ct​(xˉt​,uˉt​); the other gradient and Hessian blocks are evaluated at the same pair from the current plan. We denote the stacked gradient by cz,tc_{z,t}cz,t​ and the displayed block Hessian by czz,tc_{zz,t}czz,t​. Gradients are column vectors, matching the convention of the preceding chapters. We retain the linear terms: individual stage gradients need not vanish even at an optimal trajectory because the dynamics couple stages, and at a non-optimal plan they also drive its correction. The cxu,tc_{xu,t}cxu,t​ block measures how the marginal cost of a control changes with the state. Even if the running cost has no such cross term, eliminating later controls can create one in the quadratic tail.

The terminal cost has the same expansion, with no control coordinate:

cT(xˉT+δxT)=cT(xˉT)+pT⊤δxT+12δxT⊤PTδxT+o(∥δxT∥2),pT=∇xcT(xˉT),PT=∇xx2cT(xˉT).\begin{aligned} c_T(\bar{\mathbf x}_T+\delta\mathbf x_T) &=c_T(\bar{\mathbf x}_T)+p_T^\top\delta\mathbf x_T\\ &\quad+\frac12\delta\mathbf x_T^\top P_T\delta\mathbf x_T +o(\|\delta\mathbf x_T\|^2),\\ p_T&=\nabla_{\mathbf x}c_T(\bar{\mathbf x}_T),\qquad P_T=\nabla^2_{\mathbf x\mathbf x}c_T(\bar{\mathbf x}_T). \end{aligned}cT​(xˉT​+δxT​)pT​​=cT​(xˉT​)+pT⊤​δxT​+21​δxT⊤​PT​δxT​+o(∥δxT​∥2),=∇x​cT​(xˉT​),PT​=∇xx2​cT​(xˉT​).​
(8)

Dropping the remainders in these three Taylor expansions gives the local problem. Up to the constant ∑tcˉt+cT(xˉT)\sum_t\bar c_t+c_T(\bar{\mathbf x}_T)∑t​cˉt​+cT​(xˉT​), which does not depend on the nudges, it reads

min⁡δu1,…,δuT−1∑t=1T−1(cz,t⊤δzt+12δzt⊤czz,t δzt)+pT⊤δxT+12δxT⊤PT δxT,s.t.δxt+1=Atδxt+Btδut,t=1,…,T−1,δx1=0.\begin{aligned} \min_{\delta\mathbf u_1,\ldots,\delta\mathbf u_{T-1}}\quad &\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\Big(c_{z,t}^\top\delta\mathbf z_t +\frac12\delta\mathbf z_t^\top c_{zz,t}\,\delta\mathbf z_t\Big) +p_T^\top\delta\mathbf x_T +\frac12\delta\mathbf x_T^\top P_T\,\delta\mathbf x_T,\\ \text{s.t.}\quad &\delta\mathbf x_{t+1}=A_t\delta\mathbf x_t+B_t\delta\mathbf u_t, \quad t=1,\ldots,T-1,\\ &\delta\mathbf x_1=\mathbf0. \end{aligned}δu1​,…,δuT−1​min​s.t.​t=1∑T−1​(cz,t⊤​δzt​+21​δzt⊤​czz,t​δzt​)+pT⊤​δxT​+21​δxT⊤​PT​δxT​,δxt+1​=At​δxt​+Bt​δut​,t=1,…,T−1,δx1​=0.​
(9)

This is an LQR problem of the kind solved in the previous chapter: linear dynamics in the nudges, and a cost that is quadratic in them. Compared with the standard LQR problem it has linear cost terms and a state--control cross term, which the next section handles. Solving it gives a proposed change to the plan.

Notice what is missing from this local problem. Only the costs were expanded to second order. The dynamics were expanded to first order, so their curvature appears nowhere in (9). A general SQP method also forms a local quadratic subproblem, but not quite this one. SQP takes a quadratic model of the Lagrangian and linearizes the constraints. Here the constraints are the dynamics, so the Hessian of the Lagrangian is the cost Hessian plus the sum over iii of the multiplier λi\lambda_iλi​ times the Hessian of the iiith component of the transition. The shooting formulation is unconstrained only in the controls, because the simulator enforces the dynamics, but the local problem above still has the linearized dynamics as constraints on the nudges. iLQR is therefore SQP with the multiplier-weighted dynamics Hessians dropped. Those terms return in the DDP section, where the coefficient pt+1p_{t+1}pt+1​ of the eliminated tail plays the role of the multiplier, the costate.

Backward Elimination¶

The local problem (9) is a deterministic finite-horizon problem with linear dynamics and quadratic costs. It is an LQR problem, so the backward induction of the previous chapter solves it. This section recalls that algorithm, specializes it to LQR, and then applies the same specialization to the local problem. Each backup minimizes over one control and removes it from the problem, which is why the backward pass of iLQR is often called backward elimination.

Backward induction¶

For a deterministic problem with dynamics xt+1=ft(xt,ut)\mathbf x_{t+1}=\mathbf f_t(\mathbf x_t,\mathbf u_t)xt+1​=ft​(xt​,ut​), stage costs ctc_tct​ and terminal cost cTc_TcT​, Algorithm 1 computes the optimal cost-to-go Jt⋆J_t^\starJt⋆​ backward in time:

JT⋆(x)=cT(x),Jt⋆(x)=min⁡u[ct(x,u)+Jt+1⋆(ft(x,u))],t=T−1,…,1.\begin{aligned} J_T^\star(\mathbf x)&=c_T(\mathbf x),\\ J_t^\star(\mathbf x)&=\min_{\mathbf u}\Big[c_t(\mathbf x,\mathbf u) +J_{t+1}^\star\big(\mathbf f_t(\mathbf x,\mathbf u)\big)\Big], \qquad t=T-1,\ldots,1. \end{aligned}JT⋆​(x)Jt⋆​(x)​=cT​(x),=umin​[ct​(x,u)+Jt+1⋆​(ft​(x,u))],t=T−1,…,1.​
(10)

The minimizer at each state defines the policy πt⋆(x)\pi_t^\star(\mathbf x)πt⋆​(x). A forward pass from the initial state then applies ut=πt⋆(xt)\mathbf u_t=\pi_t^\star(\mathbf x_t)ut​=πt⋆​(xt​) and recovers the optimal trajectory. In general Jt⋆J_t^\starJt⋆​ is a function on the whole state space, which the previous chapter stored on a grid.

The LQR case: the Riccati recursion¶

With linear dynamics xt+1=Atxt+Btut\mathbf x_{t+1}=A_t\mathbf x_t+B_t\mathbf u_txt+1​=At​xt​+Bt​ut​, stage cost 12x⊤Qtx+12u⊤Rtu\tfrac12\mathbf x^\top Q_t\mathbf x+\tfrac12\mathbf u^\top R_t\mathbf u21​x⊤Qt​x+21​u⊤Rt​u and terminal cost 12x⊤QTx\tfrac12\mathbf x^\top Q_T\mathbf x21​x⊤QT​x, every cost-to-go is quadratic, Jt⋆(x)=12x⊤PtxJ_t^\star(\mathbf x)=\tfrac12\mathbf x^\top P_t\mathbf xJt⋆​(x)=21​x⊤Pt​x, so the backup only has to update a matrix. Substituting the dynamics into Jt+1⋆J_{t+1}^\starJt+1⋆​ makes the bracket a quadratic function of the stacked state and control,

12[xu] ⁣⊤[Qt+At⊤Pt+1AtAt⊤Pt+1BtBt⊤Pt+1AtRt+Bt⊤Pt+1Bt][xu].\frac12 \begin{bmatrix}\mathbf x\\\mathbf u\end{bmatrix}^{\!\top} \begin{bmatrix} Q_t+A_t^\top P_{t+1}A_t & A_t^\top P_{t+1}B_t\\ B_t^\top P_{t+1}A_t & R_t+B_t^\top P_{t+1}B_t \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}\mathbf x\\\mathbf u\end{bmatrix}.21​[xu​]⊤[Qt​+At⊤​Pt+1​At​Bt⊤​Pt+1​At​​At⊤​Pt+1​Bt​Rt​+Bt⊤​Pt+1​Bt​​][xu​].

Kt=(Rt+Bt⊤Pt+1Bt)−1Bt⊤Pt+1At,Pt=Qt+At⊤Pt+1At−At⊤Pt+1Bt(Rt+Bt⊤Pt+1Bt)−1Bt⊤Pt+1At,\begin{aligned} K_t&=(R_t+B_t^\top P_{t+1}B_t)^{-1}B_t^\top P_{t+1}A_t,\\ P_t&=Q_t+A_t^\top P_{t+1}A_t -A_t^\top P_{t+1}B_t(R_t+B_t^\top P_{t+1}B_t)^{-1}B_t^\top P_{t+1}A_t, \end{aligned}Kt​Pt​​=(Rt​+Bt⊤​Pt+1​Bt​)−1Bt⊤​Pt+1​At​,=Qt​+At⊤​Pt+1​At​−At⊤​Pt+1​Bt​(Rt​+Bt⊤​Pt+1​Bt​)−1Bt⊤​Pt+1​At​,​

Riccati for the local problem¶

The local problem has the same structure, with the nudges δxt,δut\delta\mathbf x_t,\delta\mathbf u_tδxt​,δut​ as state and control. Its terminal cost-to-go is the terminal Taylor model, and its backup is

St(δx)=min⁡δu[cz,t⊤δz+12δz⊤czz,t δz+St+1(Atδx+Btδu)],δz=(δx,δu).S_t(\delta\mathbf x)=\min_{\delta\mathbf u}\Big[ c_{z,t}^\top\delta\mathbf z+\frac12\delta\mathbf z^\top c_{zz,t}\,\delta\mathbf z +S_{t+1}(A_t\delta\mathbf x+B_t\delta\mathbf u)\Big], \qquad \delta\mathbf z=(\delta\mathbf x,\delta\mathbf u).St​(δx)=δumin​[cz,t⊤​δz+21​δz⊤czz,t​δz+St+1​(At​δx+Bt​δu)],δz=(δx,δu).
(13)

Two features differ from textbook LQR. The current plan is generally not optimal, so the local costs have linear terms, the gradients cz,tc_{z,t}cz,t​ and pTp_TpT​. The stage cost may also contain a state--control cross term cux,tc_{ux,t}cux,t​. Because of the linear terms, the cost-to-go needs a linear part as well:

St+1(δx)=st+1+pt+1⊤δx+12δx⊤Pt+1δx,S_{t+1}(\delta\mathbf x)=s_{t+1}+p_{t+1}^\top\delta\mathbf x +\frac12\delta\mathbf x^\top P_{t+1}\delta\mathbf x,St+1​(δx)=st+1​+pt+1⊤​δx+21​δx⊤Pt+1​δx,
(14)

with pTp_TpT​ and PTP_TPT​ the gradient and Hessian of cTc_TcT​ at the end of the plan. Substituting the linear dynamics into St+1S_{t+1}St+1​ makes the bracket a quadratic in δz\delta\mathbf zδz with linear coefficient qtq_tqt​ and Hessian MtM_tMt​. Written in blocks, next to the LQR matrix above,

qx,t=cx,t+At⊤pt+1,Mxx,t=cxx,t+At⊤Pt+1At,qu,t=cu,t+Bt⊤pt+1,Mux,t=cux,t+Bt⊤Pt+1At,Muu,t=cuu,t+Bt⊤Pt+1Bt.\begin{aligned} q_{x,t}&=c_{x,t}+A_t^\top p_{t+1}, & M_{xx,t}&=c_{xx,t}+A_t^\top P_{t+1}A_t,\\ q_{u,t}&=c_{u,t}+B_t^\top p_{t+1}, & M_{ux,t}&=c_{ux,t}+B_t^\top P_{t+1}A_t,\\ & & M_{uu,t}&=c_{uu,t}+B_t^\top P_{t+1}B_t. \end{aligned}qx,t​qu,t​​=cx,t​+At⊤​pt+1​,=cu,t​+Bt⊤​pt+1​,​Mxx,t​Mux,t​Muu,t​​=cxx,t​+At⊤​Pt+1​At​,=cux,t​+Bt⊤​Pt+1​At​,=cuu,t​+Bt⊤​Pt+1​Bt​.​
(15)

The Hessian blocks are the LQR blocks with QtQ_tQt​ replaced by cxx,tc_{xx,t}cxx,t​, RtR_tRt​ by cuu,tc_{uu,t}cuu,t​, and the cross term cux,tc_{ux,t}cux,t​ added. The vector qtq_tqt​ is new. In stacked form, with Ft=[At Bt]F_t=[A_t\ B_t]Ft​=[At​ Bt​], these are qt=cz,t+Ft⊤pt+1q_t=c_{z,t}+F_t^\top p_{t+1}qt​=cz,t​+Ft⊤​pt+1​ and Mt=czz,t+Ft⊤Pt+1FtM_t=c_{zz,t}+F_t^\top P_{t+1}F_tMt​=czz,t​+Ft⊤​Pt+1​Ft​. We use MtM_tMt​ for this Hessian because HtH_tHt​ denoted the Hamiltonian in the Pontryagin chapter.

Setting the control gradient to zero, Muu,tδu+Mux,tδx+qu,t=0M_{uu,t}\delta\mathbf u+M_{ux,t}\delta\mathbf x+q_{u,t}=0Muu,t​δu+Mux,t​δx+qu,t​=0, gives an affine law instead of a linear one:

δut=kt+Ktδxt,kt=−Muu,t−1qu,t,Kt=−Muu,t−1Mux,t.\delta\mathbf u_t=k_t+K_t\delta\mathbf x_t,\qquad k_t=-M_{uu,t}^{-1}q_{u,t},\qquad K_t=-M_{uu,t}^{-1}M_{ux,t}.δut​=kt​+Kt​δxt​,kt​=−Muu,t−1​qu,t​,Kt​=−Muu,t−1​Mux,t​.
(16)

The feedback gain KtK_tKt​ plays the role of the LQR gain, written here with the sign included. The feedforward term ktk_tkt​ comes from the linear terms: it changes the plan even when the state nudge is zero. Substituting the control back gives the coefficients for the preceding step,

pt=qx,t−Mux,t⊤Muu,t−1qu,t,Pt=Mxx,t−Mux,t⊤Muu,t−1Mux,t.\begin{aligned} p_t&=q_{x,t}-M_{ux,t}^\top M_{uu,t}^{-1}q_{u,t},\\ P_t&=M_{xx,t}-M_{ux,t}^\top M_{uu,t}^{-1}M_{ux,t}. \end{aligned}pt​Pt​​=qx,t​−Mux,t⊤​Muu,t−1​qu,t​,=Mxx,t​−Mux,t⊤​Muu,t−1​Mux,t​.​
(17)

The update of PtP_tPt​ is the Riccati recursion. Written out, it reads Pt=cxx,t+At⊤Pt+1At−(cux,t+Bt⊤Pt+1At)⊤(cuu,t+Bt⊤Pt+1Bt)−1(cux,t+Bt⊤Pt+1At)P_t=c_{xx,t}+A_t^\top P_{t+1}A_t-(c_{ux,t}+B_t^\top P_{t+1}A_t)^\top (c_{uu,t}+B_t^\top P_{t+1}B_t)^{-1}(c_{ux,t}+B_t^\top P_{t+1}A_t)Pt​=cxx,t​+At⊤​Pt+1​At​−(cux,t​+Bt⊤​Pt+1​At​)⊤(cuu,t​+Bt⊤​Pt+1​Bt​)−1(cux,t​+Bt⊤​Pt+1​At​), which is the LQR formula when cux,t=0c_{ux,t}=0cux,t​=0. The update of ptp_tpt​ is the new part. It carries the cost gradients backward, and with zero gradients it stays zero and ktk_tkt​ vanishes. In code, these formulas are linear solves with Muu,tM_{uu,t}Muu,t​; an explicit matrix inverse is unnecessary.

Algorithm 1 (Backward pass for the local problem)

Input: Jacobians At,BtA_t,B_tAt​,Bt​ and cost derivatives cz,t,czz,tc_{z,t},c_{zz,t}cz,t​,czz,t​ along the current plan; terminal gradient pTp_TpT​ and Hessian PTP_TPT​.

Output: Feedforward terms ktk_tkt​ and gains KtK_tKt​ for t=1,…,T−1t=1,\ldots,T-1t=1,…,T−1.

  1. For t=T−1,…,1t=T-1,\ldots,1t=T−1,…,1:

    1. Form qt=cz,t+Ft⊤pt+1q_t=c_{z,t}+F_t^\top p_{t+1}qt​=cz,t​+Ft⊤​pt+1​ and Mt=czz,t+Ft⊤Pt+1FtM_t=c_{zz,t}+F_t^\top P_{t+1}F_tMt​=czz,t​+Ft⊤​Pt+1​Ft​.

    2. Solve kt=−Muu,t−1qu,tk_t=-M_{uu,t}^{-1}q_{u,t}kt​=−Muu,t−1​qu,t​ and Kt=−Muu,t−1Mux,tK_t=-M_{uu,t}^{-1}M_{ux,t}Kt​=−Muu,t−1​Mux,t​.

    3. Update pt=qx,t−Mux,t⊤Muu,t−1qu,tp_t=q_{x,t}-M_{ux,t}^\top M_{uu,t}^{-1}q_{u,t}pt​=qx,t​−Mux,t⊤​Muu,t−1​qu,t​ and Pt=Mxx,t−Mux,t⊤Muu,t−1Mux,tP_t=M_{xx,t}-M_{ux,t}^\top M_{uu,t}^{-1}M_{ux,t}Pt​=Mxx,t​−Mux,t⊤​Muu,t−1​Mux,t​.

  2. Return ktk_tkt​ and KtK_tKt​. A forward pass from δx1=0\delta\mathbf x_1=\mathbf0δx1​=0 with δut=kt+Ktδxt\delta\mathbf u_t=k_t+K_t\delta\mathbf x_tδut​=kt​+Kt​δxt​ and δxt+1=Atδxt+Btδut\delta\mathbf x_{t+1}=A_t\delta\mathbf x_t+B_t\delta\mathbf u_tδxt+1​=At​δxt​+Bt​δut​ solves the local problem.

The tail StS_tSt​ is the cost-to-go of the local problem only. It is accurate near the current plan, and it is not a value function of the nonlinear system over its whole state space. Unlike the grid of the previous chapter, it is stored as a vector and a matrix per step, so the backward pass costs a fixed amount of work per step and grows linearly with the horizon. For linear dynamics and quadratic costs it solves the original problem exactly whenever each Muu,tM_{uu,t}Muu,t​ is positive definite. Along a nonlinear trajectory, AtA_tAt​, BtB_tBt​, and the cost derivatives describe only a local approximation. They must be recomputed after the plan changes. Exercise 1 carries out one backward pass by hand on a scalar problem.

Nonlinear Rollouts and iLQR¶

The backward pass minimizes a quadratic approximation. A large correction can make its linearized state prediction inaccurate, so a proposed control sequence must be evaluated through the original discrete simulator before it is accepted.

Starting from the same initial state, form a nonlinear trial trajectory using

x1+=xinit,ut+=uˉt+αkt+Kt(xt+−xˉt),xt+1+=ft(xt+,ut+).\begin{aligned} \mathbf x_1^+&=\mathbf x_{\mathrm{init}},\\ \mathbf u_t^+&=\bar{\mathbf u}_t+\alpha k_t +K_t(\mathbf x_t^+-\bar{\mathbf x}_t),\\ \mathbf x_{t+1}^+&=\mathbf f_t(\mathbf x_t^+,\mathbf u_t^+). \end{aligned}x1+​ut+​xt+1+​​=xinit​,=uˉt​+αkt​+Kt​(xt+​−xˉt​),=ft​(xt+​,ut+​).​
(18)

The step size α\alphaα scales the feedforward change. The feedback term responds to the state deviation that actually occurs during this trial. Its gain is not multiplied by α\alphaα. At α=0\alpha=0α=0, induction through these equations recovers the current plan, because each state deviation is then zero. For an exact linear-quadratic problem, α=1\alpha=1α=1 gives the complete solution derived by elimination.

A line search first tries α=1\alpha=1α=1, then successively smaller values. Each trial has its own nonlinear states and cost. The implementation uses 1,1/2,…,2−111,1/2,\ldots,2^{-11}1,1/2,…,2−11 and accepts a strictly lower finite cost with a small sufficient-decrease check. If

d1=∑t=1T−1qu,t⊤kt,d2=12∑t=1T−1kt⊤Muu,tkt,d_1=\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}q_{u,t}^\top k_t,\qquad d_2=\frac12\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}k_t^\top M_{uu,t}k_t,d1​=t=1∑T−1​qu,t⊤​kt​,d2​=21​t=1∑T−1​kt⊤​Muu,t​kt​,
(19)

the backward pass estimates a reduction Δ^J(α)=−αd1−α2d2\widehat\Delta J(\alpha)=-\alpha d_1-\alpha^2d_2ΔJ(α)=−αd1​−α2d2​. Acceptance requires J(Uˉ)−J(U+)≥10−4max⁡(Δ^J(α),0)J(\bar{\mathbf U})-J(\mathbf U^+)\geq10^{-4}\max(\widehat\Delta J(\alpha),0)J(Uˉ)−J(U+)≥10−4max(ΔJ(α),0) as well as a strict decrease. This estimate guides acceptance; it does not replace evaluation of the original objective.

The control curvature may be indefinite or nearly singular. Replace the matrix used in the control solve by Muu+μIM_{uu}+\mu IMuu​+μI, where μ>0\mu>0μ>0. Increasing μ\muμ makes the correction more conservative and can make the solve positive definite. The code checks a Cholesky factorization, increases μ\muμ after a failed backward pass or line search, and decreases it after an accepted step. The numerical defaults start at 10-4, multiply by ten after failure, and divide by three after acceptance, with a floor of 10-9.

When regularization changes kkk and KKK, the formulas for ptp_tpt​ and PtP_tPt​ above no longer describe substitution into the original quadratic model. The implementation therefore uses the full expressions

pt=qx+Mux⊤k+K⊤qu+K⊤Muuk,Pt=Mxx+Mux⊤K+K⊤Mux+K⊤MuuK.\begin{aligned} p_t&=q_x+M_{ux}^\top k+K^\top q_u+K^\top M_{uu}k,\\ P_t&=M_{xx}+M_{ux}^\top K+K^\top M_{ux}+K^\top M_{uu}K. \end{aligned}pt​Pt​​=qx​+Mux⊤​k+K⊤qu​+K⊤Muu​k,=Mxx​+Mux⊤​K+K⊤Mux​+K⊤Muu​K.​
(20)

Here MuuM_{uu}Muu​ is the original curvature block; regularization was used to choose the correction. These expressions also remain applicable when some controls are fixed at their bounds.

Alternating local linear-quadratic approximation, backward elimination, and nonlinear rollout gives iLQR Li & Todorov, 2004. The iteration uses second derivatives of the costs but only first derivatives of the dynamics. It is often described as a Gauss--Newton approximation to DDP. That terminology should not obscure what is approximated: the omitted terms come from dynamics curvature. If a nonlinear cost is itself a sum of squared residuals, replacing its Hessian by a residual-Jacobian product would be a further approximation; the docking code uses the exact cost Hessian.

Algorithm 2 (Successive linear-quadratic trajectory optimization)

Input: Discrete transition, running and terminal costs, initial state, and a feasible initial control sequence.

  1. Roll out the current controls and evaluate their nonlinear cost.

  2. Differentiate the transition and costs along this rollout.

  3. Starting from the terminal quadratic expansion, eliminate controls backward to obtain ktk_tkt​ and KtK_tKt​. Increase regularization and retry if a control solve fails.

  4. Test decreasing step sizes using nonlinear forward rollouts with the affine corrections.

  5. Accept a trial only when its actual cost decreases sufficiently. Otherwise increase regularization and retry the backward pass.

  6. Repeat until the control-gradient residual is small or a declared iteration or regularization limit is reached.

Output: The last accepted trajectory, its controls and local gains, an iteration history, and an explicit termination status.

The returned gains describe a neighborhood of the final plan. The docking animation below executes one stored plan. The gains used inside the optimizer do not imply that the animation replans as the boat moves.

Dynamics Curvature and DDP¶

iLQR drops the quadratic remainder in the transition’s first-order Taylor expansion. For a turning boat, a change in heading changes the direction of thrust, so products of state and control changes can affect the next state. DDP retains these second-order terms in the backward calculation.

For component iii of the transition, Taylor expansion one order further gives

δxt+1,i=(Ftδzt)i+12δzt⊤fzz,tiδzt+o(∥δzt∥2).\delta x_{t+1,i} =(F_t\delta\mathbf z_t)_i +\frac12\delta\mathbf z_t^\top f^i_{zz,t}\delta\mathbf z_t +o(\|\delta\mathbf z_t\|^2).δxt+1,i​=(Ft​δzt​)i​+21​δzt⊤​fzz,ti​δzt​+o(∥δzt​∥2).
(21)

Here fzz,tif^i_{zz,t}fzz,ti​ is the Hessian of the iiith component of ft\mathbf f_tft​ with respect to the stacked state and control, evaluated along the current plan. Substitute this expression into the same quadratic tail St+1S_{t+1}St+1​. Its linear term pt+1⊤δxt+1p_{t+1}^\top\delta\mathbf x_{t+1}pt+1⊤​δxt+1​ now contributes an additional quadratic term. Its quadratic term contributes 12δzt⊤Ft⊤Pt+1Ftδzt\tfrac12\delta\mathbf z_t^\top F_t^\top P_{t+1}F_t\delta\mathbf z_t21​δzt⊤​Ft⊤​Pt+1​Ft​δzt​; products involving the second-order part of the transition there are of order three or higher and are discarded. Consequently,

qtDDP=cz,t+Ft⊤pt+1,MtDDP=czz,t+Ft⊤Pt+1Ft+∑i=1nxpt+1,ifzz,ti.\begin{aligned} q_t^{\mathrm{DDP}}&=c_{z,t}+F_t^\top p_{t+1},\\ M_t^{\mathrm{DDP}}&=c_{zz,t}+F_t^\top P_{t+1}F_t +\sum_{i=1}^{n_x}p_{t+1,i}f^i_{zz,t}. \end{aligned}qtDDP​MtDDP​​=cz,t​+Ft⊤​pt+1​,=czz,t​+Ft⊤​Pt+1​Ft​+i=1∑nx​​pt+1,i​fzz,ti​.​
(22)

The extra contraction weights curvature of each next-state component by its linear coefficient in the eliminated tail. At a given backward stage, this is the second-order chain rule for composing the transition with that tail. These are the multiplier-weighted dynamics Hessians that the local problem left out. The tail gradient pt+1p_{t+1}pt+1​ plays the role of the SQP multiplier: it is the costate, the sensitivity of the remaining cost to the next state. In block form, the differences from iLQR are

Mxx,tDDP=cxx,t+At⊤Pt+1At+∑ipt+1,ifxx,ti,Mux,tDDP=cux,t+Bt⊤Pt+1At+∑ipt+1,ifux,ti,Muu,tDDP=cuu,t+Bt⊤Pt+1Bt+∑ipt+1,ifuu,ti.\begin{aligned} M_{xx,t}^{\mathrm{DDP}}&=c_{xx,t}+A_t^\top P_{t+1}A_t +\sum_i p_{t+1,i} f^i_{xx,t},\\ M_{ux,t}^{\mathrm{DDP}}&=c_{ux,t}+B_t^\top P_{t+1}A_t +\sum_i p_{t+1,i} f^i_{ux,t},\\ M_{uu,t}^{\mathrm{DDP}}&=c_{uu,t}+B_t^\top P_{t+1}B_t +\sum_i p_{t+1,i} f^i_{uu,t}. \end{aligned}Mxx,tDDP​Mux,tDDP​Muu,tDDP​​=cxx,t​+At⊤​Pt+1​At​+i∑​pt+1,i​fxx,ti​,=cux,t​+Bt⊤​Pt+1​At​+i∑​pt+1,i​fux,ti​,=cuu,t​+Bt⊤​Pt+1​Bt​+i∑​pt+1,i​fuu,ti​.​
(23)

Setting those three sums to zero recovers the iLQR construction. Retaining them and using the same quadratic elimination and nonlinear line search gives DDP Tassa et al., 2014. The two methods share an algorithmic structure; the curvature choice can change both the direction of a step and the amount of regularization needed to accept it. This derivation does not require solving a subproblem with quadratic dynamics constraints.

For the boat, even the continuous acceleration contains a state--control cross derivative: ∂2v˙x/(∂ψ ∂uL)=−(Fmax⁡/m)sin⁡ψ\partial^2\dot v_x/(\partial\psi\,\partial u_L) =-(F_{\max}/m)\sin\psi∂2v˙x​/(∂ψ∂uL​)=−(Fmax​/m)sinψ. The discrete derivatives used by the solver also include how heading and velocity change within the RK4 step. Automatic differentiation is applied through that complete step. A differential equation that is affine in its controls need not yield a numerical transition whose second control derivatives vanish.

The extra curvature costs computation and can be indefinite. DDP therefore still needs regularization and nonlinear acceptance tests. Neither method guarantees the globally best docking maneuver. For affine dynamics the transition Hessians are zero, so the two backward constructions coincide when all other choices agree.

Thruster Limits and Stopping Criteria¶

The boat’s controls must remain in [−1,1]2[-1,1]^2[−1,1]2, even when the unconstrained correction asks for more thrust. At zero state deviation, the feedforward step is the solution of the box-constrained quadratic problem

min⁡k qu⊤k+12k⊤(Muu+μI)k,−1−uˉt≤k≤1−uˉt.\min_k\ q_u^\top k+\frac12k^\top(M_{uu}+\mu I)k, \qquad -\mathbf1-\bar{\mathbf u}_t\leq k\leq\mathbf1-\bar{\mathbf u}_t.kmin​ qu⊤​k+21​k⊤(Muu​+μI)k,−1−uˉt​≤k≤1−uˉt​.
(24)

For two controls, each coordinate is either free, fixed at its lower bound, or fixed at its upper bound. The teaching implementation checks the nine combinations, minimizes over each face, and keeps the best feasible candidate. Positive-definite curvature makes this a strictly convex QP. Larger systems can use an active-set solver rather than enumerate all combinations Tassa et al., 2014.

The feedback rows of saturated controls are zero while their active set stays fixed. For the free coordinates F\mathcal FF, solve (Muu+μI)FFKF=−(Mux)F(M_{uu}+\mu I)_{\mathcal F\mathcal F}K_{\mathcal F} =-(M_{ux})_{\mathcal F}(Muu​+μI)FF​KF​=−(Mux​)F​. Use the full substitution formulas to update the quadratic tail. With bounds, this tail describes a neighborhood with the selected active sets; across active-set changes the minimized expression is generally piecewise quadratic. During the nonlinear trial, project the resulting control onto its box before simulation. This enforces the physical bounds when a trial leaves the neighborhood represented by the backward pass. The nonlinear cost check then decides whether that trial should be retained.

The stopping test is separate from docking success. Let g=∇UJg=\nabla_{\mathbf U}Jg=∇U​J be the gradient of the original shooting objective, computed by the adjoint recursion along the current nonlinear rollout. With normalized controls, the solver stops when

∥U−clip⁡(U−g,−1,1)∥∞≤10−5.\left\|\mathbf U-\operatorname{clip}(\mathbf U-g,-1,1)\right\|_\infty \leq10^{-5}.∥U−clip(U−g,−1,1)∥∞​≤10−5.
(25)

At an interior optimum this reduces to a small control gradient. At a bound it also allows a gradient that points toward a forbidden improvement. The experiment permits at most 120 accepted updates. If regularization exceeds 1012 without an acceptable trial, the solver retains its last accepted trajectory and reports failure to make progress. A small residual certifies approximate first-order stationarity, not a globally optimal path or a successful arrival.

Docking Trajectories and Recorded Futures¶

Do the two curvature choices produce the same maneuver from the same starting plan? Both methods receive the coasting initialization, identical costs and control limits, and the same stopping settings. The following tables report their final nonlinear costs and arrival checks. All four runs satisfy the stopping test and the docking checks: position error below 0.2 m0.2\ \mathrm m0.2 m, heading error below 3∘3^\circ3∘, speed below 0.05 m/s0.05\ \mathrm{m/s}0.05 m/s, angular speed below 1∘/s1^\circ/\mathrm s1∘/s, bounded thrust, and positive hull clearance. The maximum position difference between the planning trajectory and the finer replay is below 10−6 m10^{-6}\ \mathrm m10−6 m in these runs. Clearance is checked on the finer grid; this remains a sampled validation, not a proof of continuous-time collision avoidance.

In the angled approach, iLQR reaches cost 8.0515 in 18 accepted updates, while DDP reaches a different stationary trajectory with cost 11.9879 in 34 updates. The DDP trajectory makes two full turns near the berth. Its final unwrapped heading is approximately 720∘720^\circ720∘, which the periodic heading cost treats as the same orientation as zero. Reaching this stationary trajectory does not remove the extra motion accumulated on the way there. In the sideways-drift case, both reach cost 7.6674, with 13 accepted updates for iLQR and 45 for DDP. These are outcomes of two particular local solves, not a general ranking of the algorithms. The difference in the first case also shows why comparing iteration counts alone can hide a difference in the solutions obtained.

Within one selected plan, simulation time has a different meaning from optimizer iteration. At two seconds, for example, the boat occupies the two-second state of that rollout. Its remaining states give a prediction of where it will go if the rest of the stored controls are applied. Outlines spaced equally in time spread apart while the boat is moving quickly and cluster as it comes to rest. Reverse thrust helps remove momentum before arrival.

The replay reads recorded simulations, so exploring it does not rerun an optimizer. Recomputing a plan from newly observed states is the additional step introduced in receding-horizon control.

Pulling Down a Thermoacoustic Refrigerator¶

A standing-wave thermoacoustic refrigerator is a sealed, gas-filled tube with a loudspeaker at one end and a stack of thin parallel plates inside (Figure 8a). The loudspeaker excites a standing sound wave in the tube. Each gas parcel near a plate is pushed back and forth along it, compressing and heating as it moves toward the loudspeaker end and expanding and cooling as it moves away. At the loudspeaker end of its travel the parcel is warmer than the plate and gives up heat to it; at the far end it is cooler than the plate and takes heat from it. Every cycle therefore moves a little heat one step along the plate, and the parcels together act as a bucket brigade that transports heat from the far end of the stack toward the loudspeaker end. Sound is used to move heat from a cold place to a warmer one, against the direction it would flow on its own. A household heat pump does the same thing with a compressor when it extracts heat from cold outdoor air and delivers it indoors; a refrigerator is the same machine used for its cold side. A cold heat exchanger at the far end of the stack connects to the payload, the refrigeration term for the object or compartment being cooled, and a hot heat exchanger at the loudspeaker end rejects the heat to ambient air. There are no moving parts other than the loudspeaker, and the only knob is how hard it drives. The control problem is what refrigeration engineers call a pull-down: bringing the payload from ambient temperature down to its set point after switch-on. Here that means choosing a driver-amplitude schedule that brings the payload to a target temperature by a fixed deadline while spending little acoustic energy.

In the online book, the replay reads the recorded plans and integrates only the constant-amplitude comparison; it does not rerun the optimizer.

Rather than simulate the acoustics, we lump the whole device into two thermal masses (Figure 8b): the cold exchanger together with its payload, and the hot exchanger. The state is their temperatures, xt=(Tc,t,Th,t)\mathbf x_t=(T_{c,t},T_{h,t})xt​=(Tc,t​,Th,t​), and the action is the normalized driver amplitude ut∈[0,1]u_t\in[0,1]ut​∈[0,1], so this is a two-dimensional continuous-state, one-dimensional continuous-action problem. Let ΔT=Th−Tc\Delta T=T_h-T_cΔT=Th​−Tc​ be the temperature span across the stack and η(ΔT)=1−ΔT/ΔT0\eta(\Delta T)=1-\Delta T/\Delta T_0η(ΔT)=1−ΔT/ΔT0​ a pumping efficiency that decreases linearly with that span. The continuous-time dynamics are

Q˙c=kqu2η(ΔT),W˙=kwu2η(ΔT)+kvu2+k3u3,CcT˙c=−Q˙c+Qload,ChT˙h=Q˙c+W˙−UA(Th−Tamb).\begin{aligned} \dot Q_c &= k_q u^2\eta(\Delta T),& \dot W &= k_w u^2\eta(\Delta T)+k_vu^2+k_3u^3,\\ C_c\dot T_c &= -\dot Q_c+Q_{\mathrm{load}},& C_h\dot T_h &= \dot Q_c+\dot W-UA(T_h-T_{\mathrm{amb}}). \end{aligned}Q˙​c​Cc​T˙c​​=kq​u2η(ΔT),=−Q˙​c​+Qload​,​W˙Ch​T˙h​​=kw​u2η(ΔT)+kv​u2+k3​u3,=Q˙​c​+W˙−UA(Th​−Tamb​).​
(26)

Here Q˙c\dot Q_cQ˙​c​ is the heat pumped out of the cold side, W˙\dot WW˙ is the acoustic work the driver injects, QloadQ_{\mathrm{load}}Qload​ is a parasitic heat leak into the payload, and UAUAUA is the hot exchanger’s conductance to ambient. Both heat flows scale with u2u^2u2 because acoustic power is quadratic in wave amplitude, and both weaken as the span grows; this is the short-stack approximation of thermoacoustics Swift, 1988Swift, 2017. Two loss terms complete the work: a viscous term in u2u^2u2 and a cubic term k3u3k_3u^3k3​u3 that makes hard driving disproportionately expensive. The coupling matters for the optimizer. Driving hard pumps heat faster, but it also dumps that heat plus the work into the hot side, which raises ThT_hTh​, widens the span, and lowers the efficiency of every later step. Refrigeration engineers measure this efficiency by the coefficient of performance (COP), the ratio Q˙c/W˙\dot Q_c/\dot WQ˙​c​/W˙ of heat pumped to work spent while the driver is on. Unlike an efficiency it can exceed one, because the work only moves heat rather than producing cold. In this model the COP falls as the span grows and, through the cubic term, as the amplitude grows; one scenario below removes the cubic term so that the COP no longer depends on amplitude. All coefficients are synthetic teaching values, not measurements of a particular device.

The stage cost charges only energy, and the target enters only through the terminal cost, so the objective is sparse in the RL sense: nothing tells the optimizer how cold to be at intermediate times. The terminal penalty is soft, so a plan can trade some arrival error for lower energy. Both methods start from the constant open-loop sequence ut=0.5u_t=0.5ut​=0.5 and use the same action bounds and stopping settings.

For comparison, constant full amplitude in the baseline case ends at 2.20 °C, uses 1426 J, and has cost 149.89.

The baseline plan drives relatively hard at first, eases off, then ramps to full amplitude near the deadline. Early driving uses the initially small temperature span, but it also warms the hot side and weakens later pumping. The fixed load adds the same total heat over every 300-second plan. Control timing still changes the temperature span and therefore the final cold temperature. Running at full amplitude throughout uses about 1426 J1426\ \mathrm J1426 J and reaches 2.20 ∘C2.20\ ^\circ\mathrm C2.20 ∘C; its nonlinear cost is 149.886, versus 51.224 for the baseline local plan. The soft terminal cost need not favor the coldest possible final state.

Without the parasitic load, a nearly constant amplitude is economical. To see the tendency, temporarily hold the temperature span fixed and write v=u2v=u^2v=u2. Heat pumped is then proportional to vvv, while the cubic loss is proportional to v3/2v^{3/2}v3/2, a convex function for v≥0v\geq0v≥0. For a fixed total amount of pumping, Jensen’s inequality favors spreading vvv through time. The actual schedule is not exactly constant because the span and hot-side temperature still respond to the controls. With Ch=200 J/KC_h=200\ \mathrm{J/K}Ch​=200 J/K and UA=0.2 W/KUA=0.2\ \mathrm{W/K}UA=0.2 W/K, the amplitude rises through most of the horizon, then turns off for the final two intervals. Both thermal storage and heat rejection changed in that experiment, so it does not isolate the effect of either parameter.

The DDP curvature term also has a direct physical interpretation here. For the continuous cold-side equation,

∂2T˙c∂u ∂ΔT=2kquCcΔT0.\frac{\partial^2\dot T_c}{\partial u\,\partial\Delta T} =\frac{2k_qu}{C_c\Delta T_0}.∂u∂ΔT∂2T˙c​​=Cc​ΔT0​2kq​u​.
(28)

Increasing the temperature span weakens pumping, and this mixed derivative measures how that effect changes with amplitude. The solver differentiates the complete RK4 transition, whose Hessian also contains effects from the intermediate integration stages.

When k3=0k_3=0k3​=0, both pumping and work are quadratic in amplitude at a fixed temperature span. Their instantaneous ratio then no longer depends on amplitude, leaving weaker preferences among some schedules. In the recorded run, iLQR reaches its iteration limit while DDP satisfies the stopping test; both reach nearly the same final cost. For the sluggish hot side, DDP reaches a different, slightly lower-cost local plan than iLQR. Lowering the target to 0 ∘C0\ ^\circ\mathrm C0 ∘C produces a plan saturated at ut=1u_t=1ut​=1 throughout the fixed horizon, exercising the box-constrained backward step. These outcomes depend on the initial sequence. Starting the baseline from constant amplitudes 0.1 and 0.9 leads to other local plans, so neither result certifies a global minimum.

Exercises¶

Exercise 1 (Backward induction by hand)

Consider a scalar problem with T=3T=3T=3, initial state x1=0x_1=0x1​=0, dynamics xt+1=xt+utx_{t+1}=x_t+u_txt+1​=xt​+ut​, and cost

J=12u12+12u22+β2(x3−r)2,β>0.J=\frac12u_1^2+\frac12u_2^2+\frac\beta2(x_3-r)^2,\qquad \beta>0.J=21​u12​+21​u22​+2β​(x3​−r)2,β>0.
(29)

  1. Treat x2x_2x2​ as given, substitute x3=x2+u2x_3=x_2+u_2x3​=x2​+u2​, and minimize over u2u_2u2​. Write the minimizing u2u_2u2​ as a function of x2x_2x2​ and compute the remaining cost-to-go.

  2. Use x2=u1x_2=u_1x2​=u1​ to minimize over u1u_1u1​. Find both controls and the terminal state.

  3. For β=r=1\beta=r=1β=r=1, check that u1=u2=1/3u_1=u_2=1/3u1​=u2​=1/3, x3=2/3x_3=2/3x3​=2/3, and J=1/6J=1/6J=1/6. Why is the final position short of rrr?

  4. Why is it useful that step 1 returns u2u_2u2​ as a function of x2x_2x2​ rather than as a number? What happens as β→∞\beta\to\inftyβ→∞?

Solution to Exercise 1

The last control is u2=β(r−x2)/(1+β)u_2=\beta(r-x_2)/(1+\beta)u2​=β(r−x2​)/(1+β), and its minimized tail is β(x2−r)2/[2(1+β)]\beta(x_2-r)^2/[2(1+\beta)]β(x2​−r)2/[2(1+β)]. With x1=0x_1=0x1​=0, minimizing the remaining expression gives u1=βr/(1+2β)u_1=\beta r/(1+2\beta)u1​=βr/(1+2β), followed by the same value for u2u_2u2​. Thus x3=2βr/(1+2β)x_3=2\beta r/(1+2\beta)x3​=2βr/(1+2β). For β=r=1\beta=r=1β=r=1 this gives u1=u2=1/3u_1=u_2=1/3u1​=u2​=1/3 and x3=2/3x_3=2/3x3​=2/3, so J=118+118+118=1/6J=\tfrac1{18}+\tfrac1{18}+\tfrac1{18}=1/6J=181​+181​+181​=1/6. The final position falls short because the objective trades terminal error against effort; arrival is penalized, not imposed as an equality.

The function u2(x2)u_2(x_2)u2​(x2​) is a feedback law: if the state reaching the last step changes, the minimizing last control changes with it. In the vector case this dependence becomes the gain KtK_tKt​. As the terminal weight grows, the two controls tend to r/2r/2r/2 and the terminal state tends to rrr.

Exercise 2 (The linear-quadratic special case)

Suppose the dynamics are affine and every cost is quadratic, with a strictly convex reduced objective and no control bounds. Explain why one unregularized backward pass and a full nonlinear rollout solve the problem from any feasible initial trajectory. What changes when using DDP?

Solution to Exercise 2

The local expansions are exact. Backward elimination therefore minimizes the original quadratic problem in perturbation coordinates, and α=1\alpha=1α=1 recovers its solution. The affine simulator agrees exactly with the linearized perturbation dynamics. All transition Hessians vanish, so DDP produces the same correction. This is also a useful implementation test: compare the returned controls with a dense solve of the reduced quadratic objective.

Exercise 3 (A curvature term in the boat model)

Temporarily discretize the boat with forward Euler. Derive the mixed derivative ∂2fvx/(∂ψ ∂uL)\partial^2 f^{v_x}/(\partial\psi\,\partial u_L)∂2fvx​/(∂ψ∂uL​). Identify where it enters the DDP backward pass and why iLQR omits it.

Solution to Exercise 3

The Euler velocity update contains h(Fmax⁡/m)(uL+uR)cos⁡ψh(F_{\max}/m)(u_L+u_R)\cos\psih(Fmax​/m)(uL​+uR​)cosψ. The mixed derivative is therefore −h(Fmax⁡/m)sin⁡ψ-h(F_{\max}/m)\sin\psi−h(Fmax​/m)sinψ. DDP multiplies it by the vxv_xvx​ component of pt+1p_{t+1}pt+1​ and adds it to the corresponding state--control curvature entry. iLQR uses the first-order transition, whose second derivatives are zero within the local model. The actual experiment differentiates RK4 instead, so its mixed derivative includes the intermediate integration stages.

Exercise 4 (Remove the stopping penalty)

Set the terminal translational-velocity weight to zero and rerun the angled approach. Compare position error, terminal speed, and controls with the default run. Repeat with an eight-second horizon. Does arriving near the berth imply that docking succeeded?

Solution to Exercise 4

Use make_problem(velocity_weight=0.) and keep every other choice fixed for the first comparison. For the shorter experiment, set steps=80 in BoatParameters and regenerate the initial controls. Removing the terminal velocity term removes an explicit incentive to stop at the final time. Running position and velocity costs can still lead to a slow arrival, especially over the longer horizon, so failure is not inevitable. Measure the final speed independently of position error and retain the same docking tolerances for both objectives. A low-cost pass through the target is not a successful stationary arrival.

Exercise 5 (Saturation and a rejected step)

For a positive-definite 2×22\times22×2 matrix MMM with nonzero off-diagonal entries, compare the exact box-QP solution with clipping −M−1q-M^{-1}q−M−1q componentwise. Explain why they can differ. What should the trajectory optimizer retain if every nonlinear trial is rejected?

Solution to Exercise 5

Fixing one coordinate at a bound changes the stationarity equation for the other coordinate through the off-diagonal entry of MMM. Componentwise clipping does not solve that new equation. The face minimization does. If no nonlinear trial is accepted, the solver retains its previous controls and states and reports that it could not make progress; it must not replace them with an unaccepted trial or report convergence from rejection alone.

Exercise 6 (Thermal load and amplitude scheduling)

Set the parasitic cold-side load to zero and rerun the baseline refrigerator problem. Explain why the optimized amplitude becomes nearly constant, using the convexity of the cubic loss. Then restore the load and double the horizon to 600 s600\ \mathrm s600 s. Predict how the amplitude schedule and energy use change.

Solution to Exercise 6

With no load, cooling obtained early is not directly undone by a constant heat leak. If the temperature span were fixed, a given amount of cooling would fix the sum of vt=ut2v_t=u_t^2vt​=ut2​. The cubic loss is proportional to vt3/2v_t^{3/2}vt3/2​, so Jensen’s inequality favors equal vtv_tvt​ across time. The temperature span still evolves, which explains the modest variation in the computed schedule. With the load restored, the longer horizon admits lower amplitude over more intervals, but the leak adds heat throughout that extra time. In this model, the 600 s600\ \mathrm s600 s local solution starts near 0.59, reaches 0.89 by 550 s550\ \mathrm s550 s, and uses full amplitude in the final intervals. Its approximately 1392 J1392\ \mathrm J1392 J of energy exceeds the shorter baseline’s use.

Run uv run python scripts/build_thermoacoustic_pulldown_artifacts.py to regenerate the refrigerator results table, figures, diagnostics, and the browser replay data.

Summary and Outlook¶

A feasible nonlinear rollout supplies the point around which dynamics and costs are approximated. Backward elimination of a local quadratic problem then supplies both a feedforward change and a state-dependent correction. iLQR repeats that calculation with linearized dynamics; DDP includes the second-order chain-rule terms from the transition. Nonlinear rollouts, regularization, and acceptance tests connect these local calculations to a decreasing sequence of actual trajectory costs. The refrigerator applies the same calculation to a bounded driver amplitude, with energy use and terminal temperature competing in the objective.

The quadratic tail produced by elimination is a local model of the cost-to-go along one trajectory. For linear-quadratic problems it is the optimal cost-to-go itself. When the model prescribes a distribution over successors instead of one next state, stochastic dynamic programming replaces the continuation cost by a conditional expectation.
